video_title: Explosive Growth of Private Markets with Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane | LFTC
gist: Hamilton Lane CEO Erik Hirsch tells Michael Batnick that private equity is correlated with public equity, manager dispersion remains wide, private credit data shows about 2 percent defaults despite retail redemptions, and secondary day-one markups follow accounting rules. He argues the public market is undervaluing alt managers and that private access is needed as companies stay private.

insights.claim: Private equity returns are correlated with public equity; the appearance of low correlation comes from the reporting time lag of at least a quarter in LP statements and disappears when the lag is removed.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Do not count private equity as diversifying at face value; smoothed marks understate risk.
insights.quote: It's totally correlated to the private to the public markets

insights.claim: The 1980s era of buying private companies at large illiquidity discounts with easy leverage is long gone, so there is not alpha for everyone in private markets, though different exposures like infrastructure differ from S&P 500 constituents.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Private allocations should be justified by exposure and manager skill, not a structural discount.

insights.claim: Despite predictions that returns would compress as more capital arrived, dispersion from top to bottom manager is about as wide today as 20 years ago in venture, private equity and private credit.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Manager selection dominates outcomes, and an index approach to privates is inappropriate.
insights.quote: The dispersion of performance from kind of top to bottom is basically as big today as it was 20 years ago

insights.claim: Purchase price is not the main determinant of private equity outcomes; what the owner and management do with the asset after purchase drives results, which is why dispersion is so wide.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Operating skill rather than entry valuation explains PE return differences.

insights.claim: Most Hamilton Lane clients invest in far fewer than 10 funds per year, since each fund holds 10 to 30 or more companies, so eight funds gives hundreds of holdings; Hamilton Lane sees around 1,500 funds in market and narrows them to a client's six.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Diversification in privates requires few funds; selection, not breadth, is the work.

insights.claim: Access and diligence are asymmetric: top managers compress fundraising and only go to a few sources so about 90 percent of investors never see them, and larger investors get deeper diligence information than small ones.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Retail and small investors face adverse selection in private funds.
insights.quote: So this is a very asymmetrical industry. It's not fair.

insights.claim: Only about 20 large firms have viable franchises raising capital from individual investors; thousands of institutional-only managers will live or die on institutional returns.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: The retail wave benefits a few big managers, and the mass of small GPs still depends on institutional LPs.

themes.theme: Private credit stress and retail flows

insights.claim: Post-COVID euphoria led to high prices, questionable underwriting and remote diligence; industry returns have lagged public markets for 3 to 5 years, distributions relative to NAV are down and holding periods are rising, though vintage-year dispersion shows not everyone behaved that way.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Liquidity, not headline returns, is the current weakness in private equity.

insights.claim: Fundraising charts that show declines are closed-end only and omit evergreen vehicles and secondaries, so they overstate the drop; retail entry is driven by structure and regulation changes and only partly offsets institutional fundraising pressure.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Check what a private-markets fundraising chart excludes before drawing conclusions.

insights.claim: Private credit shone in 2022 because floating-rate loans avoided duration losses while bonds fell about 15 percent, returning roughly 10 to 12 percent, which drew capital rapidly.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Explains the vintage of retail-driven private credit inflows and expectations.

insights.claim: Private credit exists because regional banks pulled back from lending to small private businesses, and capital needs did not disappear; growth then spawned many spin-out managers who had never operated in a down cycle.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Structural demand is real but manager quality is diluted and untested through a cycle.

insights.claim: No 'cockroach' wave has appeared yet: default rates are around 2 percent, bankruptcies are not rising materially, big public managers report little PIK shift; some portfolios do have problems (software exposure, weak lending standards).
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Current data do not support a broad private credit crisis, but dispersion means picking managers matters.
insights.quote: we haven't really seen the data bear that out yet

insights.claim: Media coverage of private credit is heavy on speculation and one-off anonymous sources and light on hard data, and the headlines have spooked individual investors into redemptions.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Redemption pressure may be sentiment-driven rather than fundamental.

insights.claim: Apollo Debt Solutions BDC, about $26 billion, capped withdrawals at 5 percent of shares after 14.7 percent of shares sought to redeem, down from 16.8 percent the prior quarter.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Concrete gauge of semi-liquid vehicle redemption pressure easing slightly but still triple the cap.

insights.claim: Advisers face asymmetric career risk: holding a client through a drawdown risks being fired, while returning the dollar risks little and may look heroic, which drives redemption from credit funds by nervous investors.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Adviser incentives amplify redemption waves in semi-liquid funds.

insights.claim: Institutions are still allocating to private credit; a sophisticated pension fund seeded Hamilton Lane's new semi-liquid credit product amid the negative headlines, and Hirsch notes investors redeemed credit funds while subscribing to equity funds even though bad credit implies worse equity.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Institutional behavior diverges from retail, and the retail rotation is internally inconsistent.

insights.claim: Hirsch expects retail behavior to steady as data, maturity and adviser experience grow, comparing it to advisers who now tell clients to ride out public-market panics.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Redemption gating may ease as the investor base matures.

insights.claim: Day-one secondary markups are an industry accounting practice: a buyer of a passive LP interest must carry it at the GP's mark, so a position bought at 65 cents can be held at a dollar.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Reported gains on secondary purchases reflect accounting rules and stale GP marks, not necessarily realized value.

insights.claim: Secondary discounts now average about 13 percent, down from much larger discounts around 2000 when Hamilton Lane did its first deal and buyers were few.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Increased competition has compressed secondary entry discounts to reasonable levels.

insights.claim: Valuation timing lags matter in secondaries: a deal priced in mid-September off March valuations closes months later and lands on books using a September valuation.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Reported secondary returns depend heavily on the valuation date mismatch.

insights.claim: Hamilton Lane invests in under 1 percent of the secondary deal flow it sees and emphasizes portfolio construction.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Selectivity is claimed as the edge in a competitive secondary market.

insights.claim: Hamilton Lane reported nearly $640 million net inflows in the June quarter, over $19 billion of semi-liquid AUM, no gates, and positive net inflows in 10 of 12 semi-liquid funds, against about $146 billion AUM and over $1 trillion including advisory assets.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Hamilton Lane shows inflows while peers face outflows.

insights.claim: Hamilton Lane's incentive fees reached $175 million for fiscal 2026 so far versus about $54 million in 2022, yet the stock is down almost by half, like other alternative manager stocks.
insights.speaker: host Michael Batnick
insights.so_what: Public alt manager equities are pricing skepticism despite rising fee earnings.
insights.quote: your stock has almost been cut in half

insights.claim: Hirsch says the public market swings to extremes and is skeptical that alternative manager earnings can continue; the firm has been buying back stock and he is buying personally.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Management signals value at current prices, a bullish insider-alignment datapoint.

insights.claim: Leaving private markets means putting every dollar in increasingly correlated, mega-cap, AI-driven public equities, and companies can stay private forever, so value creation in firms like SpaceX and Anthropic accrues to private holders before they reach trillion-dollar valuations.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Argument that private access is needed for exposure to the growth economy as IPOs shrink.
insights.quote: The money is not going to get made in a major way by the public holders.

insights.claim: Some Hamilton Lane funds are tokenized with minimums as low as about $500 and are available directly through platforms as well as through advisers.
insights.speaker: guest Erik Hirsch, CEO of Hamilton Lane
insights.so_what: Access barriers for retail investors in privates are falling.
